title: Modified Accrual & Governmental Fund Statements
description: Explain modified accrual & governmental fund statements.
html:
Modified Accrual Accounting

Modified Accrual Accounting

Governmental funds use the modified accrual basis of accounting together with the current financial resources measurement focus.

The key question is not simply whether revenue has been earned. Governmental funds focus on whether financial resources are available to finance current-period expenditures.

Revenue Recognition

Under modified accrual, revenue is generally recognized when it is:

MEASURABLE + AVAILABLE = RECOGNIZE REVENUE

Measurable

Revenue is measurable when the government can reasonably determine the amount.

Available

Available generally means the revenue is collectible within the current period or soon enough afterward to pay liabilities of the current period.

The exact availability period can depend on the government's policy and the type of revenue.

Property Tax Example

Assume a government levies property taxes of $500,000.

At year-end, $470,000 qualifies for recognition under the government's measurable-and-available criteria.

The remaining $30,000 is measurable but is not expected to be collected soon enough to satisfy the government's availability criterion.

Revenue Recognized $470,000
Not Yet Recognized as Revenue $30,000

The unavailable portion is generally reported as a deferred inflow of resources rather than current-period governmental fund revenue.

Expenditures

Governmental funds generally recognize expenditures rather than expenses.

Expenditures are generally recognized when a related fund liability is incurred, subject to important exceptions for certain long-term items.

Because governmental funds focus on current financial resources, certain expenditures related to long-term obligations are generally recognized when payment is due or when the obligation is expected to require the use of current financial resources.

Governmental Funds Expenditures
Government-Wide Statements Expenses

Capital Asset Purchase

Suppose a governmental fund purchases equipment for $100,000.

In the governmental fund financial statements:

$100,000 CAPITAL OUTLAY EXPENDITURE

The governmental fund generally does not record the equipment as a capital asset.

At the government-wide level, however, the equipment is generally capitalized and subsequently depreciated.

Long-Term Debt Proceeds

Suppose a governmental fund receives $1,000,000 from issuing long-term bonds.

The governmental fund generally does not recognize a long-term liability for the bonds. Instead, the proceeds are generally reported as an other financing source.

BOND PROCEEDS ≠ GOVERNMENTAL FUND REVENUE BOND PROCEEDS = OTHER FINANCING SOURCE

The long-term liability is generally reported in the government-wide financial statements.

Principal Payments

When a governmental fund pays principal on general long-term debt, the payment is generally reported as an expenditure.

This differs from accrual accounting, where repayment of principal reduces a liability rather than creating an expense.

Modified Accrual vs. Accrual

Governmental Funds Current Financial Resources + Modified Accrual
Government-Wide Economic Resources + Accrual

CPA Memory Rules

  • Revenue → measurable + available.
  • Governmental funds → expenditures, not expenses.
  • Capital asset purchase → expenditure in governmental funds.
  • Long-term bond proceeds → other financing source in governmental funds.
  • Governmental funds generally do not report general capital assets or general long-term liabilities.
GOVERNMENTAL FUND Revenue = Measurable + Available Capital Purchase = Expenditure Bond Proceeds = Other Financing Source

Key Takeaway

When you see a governmental fund question, think about current financial resources. This explains why modified accrual treatment differs from normal business accrual accounting.

Governmental Fund Financial Statements

Governmental Fund Financial Statements

Governmental funds generally present two major financial statements:

Balance Sheet Assets + Deferred Outflows of Resources − Liabilities − Deferred Inflows of Resources = Fund Balance
Operating Statement Revenues − Expenditures + Other Financing Sources/Uses

Governmental Funds Balance Sheet

The governmental funds balance sheet reflects the current financial resources measurement focus.

Therefore, it generally reports current financial assets and related liabilities rather than the government's complete economic resources.

Usually NOT Reported Here

  • General capital assets
  • General long-term liabilities

Those items are generally reported in the government-wide financial statements instead.

Fund Balance Classifications

Governmental fund balance is classified according to the nature of constraints placed on how resources may be used.

Nonspendable Not in Spendable Form or Legally Required to Remain Intact
Restricted Externally Enforceable Restrictions
Committed Constraint Imposed by Government's Highest-Level Decision-Making Authority
Assigned Intended for a Particular Purpose
Unassigned Residual Classification

Nonspendable Fund Balance

Resources are nonspendable when they cannot currently be spent because they are not in spendable form or must legally remain intact.

Examples

Inventories, prepaid items, and the principal of certain permanent funds may be nonspendable.

Restricted Fund Balance

Restricted fund balance results from constraints imposed by external parties or through law.

Example

Grant money that may legally be used only for a specified program may be restricted.

Committed vs. Assigned

Committed resources are constrained by formal action of the government's highest-level decision-making authority.

Assigned resources reflect an intended use but do not meet the stronger criteria for restricted or committed classification.

Unassigned Fund Balance

Unassigned fund balance is generally the residual classification for the General Fund.

Unassigned fund balance is generally used as the residual classification in the General Fund. Other governmental funds may report a negative unassigned amount when expenditures exceed amounts available in the classifications applicable to that fund.

Statement of Revenues, Expenditures, and Changes in Fund Balances

This statement explains how governmental fund balances changed during the period.

REVENUES − EXPENDITURES = EXCESS (DEFICIENCY) OF REVENUES OVER EXPENDITURES + OTHER FINANCING SOURCES − OTHER FINANCING USES = NET CHANGE IN FUND BALANCE

Other Financing Sources and Uses

Certain financing transactions are reported separately from revenues and expenditures.

  • Proceeds from long-term debt are generally an other financing source.
  • Transfers in are generally other financing sources.
  • Transfers out are generally other financing uses.

Quick Example

Assume a governmental fund reports:

Revenues $900,000
Expenditures $820,000
Bond Proceeds $150,000
Transfer Out $30,000
$900,000 − $820,000 + $150,000 − $30,000 = $200,000 Net Increase in Fund Balance

CPA Exam Traps

  • Bond proceeds are not governmental fund revenue.
  • Transfers are not revenues or expenditures.
  • General capital assets generally do not appear on the governmental funds balance sheet.
  • General long-term debt generally does not appear as a governmental fund long-term liability.

Memory Rule

GOVERNMENTAL FUNDS: Balance Sheet → Current Financial Resources Operating Statement → Revenues + Expenditures Financing → Other Financing Sources / Uses

Key Takeaway

Keep governmental fund reporting separate from government-wide reporting. The fund statements emphasize current financial resources, while government-wide statements later convert the information to an economic-resources perspective.
objectives: Explain modified accrual & governmental fund statements.
Prepare and reconcile appropriate governmental reporting amounts.

quiz.prompt: Under modified accrual accounting, revenue is generally recognized when it is:

choices.text: Earned and collectible within five years

quiz.explanation: Governmental fund revenue generally must be both measurable and available.
